forecasts.label: Interest payable
forecasts.note: The council's own full-year forecast, restated at each quarterly return.

forecasts.label: Revenue spending (net current expenditure)
forecasts.note: The full-year forecast of net current expenditure — the running cost of services — restated each quarter against the same measure at outturn.

forecasts.label: Capital expenditure
forecasts.note: Total capital spending forecast each quarter (the capital payments return) against the annual capital outturn. Capital spending not met from grants or receipts is what turns into new borrowing, so a forecast running ahead of outturn is a borrowing signal.

in_year.label: Interest payable, as reported each quarter
in_year.note: Per quarter, not cumulative. The quarterly return is a lighter collection than the annual one and sums to roughly 92% of it nationally, so the two are shown apart rather than added together.

news_drafts.headline: Kingston pension fund reports regulatory breach after missing 31 August benefit statement deadline
news_drafts.lead:
Kingston upon Thames's pension fund could not produce annual benefit statements that comply with the McCloud age-discrimination ruling by the statutory deadline of 31 August, the Pension Board's papers for 14 October show. They record the outcome as "a regulatory breach being reported to The Pensions Regulator".

The papers give the cause as ongoing delays in receiving software patches. The fund's administration system cannot yet process the bulk McCloud recalculations. Risk 21 on the fund's risk register, which covers the software provider's failure to deliver software compliant with the Local Government Pension Scheme, is rated red.

Officers are keeping the risk at red until the remaining system upgrades are delivered, fully tested and verified.

news_drafts.headline: Kingston forecasts £18.18m schools overspend in 2026/27, taking the special needs deficit to £38.72m
news_drafts.lead:
Kingston upon Thames council expects to spend £235.61m this year on services funded by the dedicated schools grant (the government grant that funds schools), against a grant of £219.23m. That is an in-year shortfall of £18.18m, according to the budget monitoring report (the in-year check of spending against budget) at month four, which went to the Corporate and Resources Committee on 24 September. The cumulative deficit is projected to reach £38.72m by the end of the year, before any government write-off.

The report puts £18.42m of the overspend in high needs, the part of school funding for children with special educational needs and disabilities. It attributes this to rising demand set against government funding frozen at 2025/26 levels. The borough had 2,236 education, health and care plans at the end of June 2026, up 8% on a year earlier.

The Department for Education has introduced a High Needs Stability Grant, which is expected to write off 90% of the deficit carried from last year, which stood at £20.52m in March 2026. That depends on approval of the government's SEND reform plan, expected in September 2026. For deficits building up in 2026/27 and 2027/28, the report says there is "not yet clarity". The department has said it will take "an appropriate and proportionate approach", but that support will not be "unlimited".

news_drafts.headline: Kingston upon Thames pension fund faces 1 January 2028 statutory deadline with unresolved software defects preventing benefit recalculation for 3,483 members
news_drafts.lead: Kingston upon Thames's pension fund is racing against a 1 January 2028 statutory deadline to recalculate benefits for 3,483 members under a legally required reform, but faces a critical software dependency with no confirmed delivery dates. The core system was delivered in July 2025 but defects prevent accurate benefit calculations. The supplier has said patches will fix the issue, but dates remain unconfirmed. Officers rate this a red risk (the highest level) because the work cannot proceed without the patches. The council is using a standalone calculator to ensure members retiring or dying immediately have correct benefits calculated while waiting. The delay stems from industry-wide defects affecting multiple public sector pension funds pressing suppliers for fixes.

findings.headline: The Fund is 'largely compliant' with the updated LGPS governance requirements, with a Senior LGPS Officer to be appointed by 31 December 2026.
findings.detail: The paper says a shared Senior LGPS Officer is being recruited, with Sutton Council's Strategy and Resources Committee approval sought in November and the appointment effective from 1 December. An Independent Person must also be appointed by 31 December 2026, and the first Independent Governance Review must be completed by March 2028.
findings.matters: Mandatory appointments with fixed statutory deadlines under the new LGPS governance rules are a compliance point that finance directors across the sector are working to the same dates on.

findings.headline: £502.7m is invested directly in London CIV pooled funds and £414.7m indirectly, together 60.6% of the Fund's assets at 30 June 2026.
findings.detail: The paper says the assets not under LCIV management are legacy property and active equity holdings with Fidelity and Columbia Threadneedle. Those active equity holdings are expected to transition into LCIV's new Global Core Equity fund in September or October 2026.
findings.matters: The share of assets still outside the pool is the measure a peer council would use to judge how far it has got through Fit for the Future pooling.

findings.headline: The Fund is expected to stay cashflow negative for the next three years, becoming more so by 2028/29, as contribution rates fall.
findings.detail: The paper says the change in cashflow is largely driven by a reduction in employer contribution rates from 1 April 2026, following the 2025 valuation. findings.matters: Employer contribution income falling while benefit outflows rise is a pressure on any LGPS fund that a finance director would need to plan cashflow around.
